grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: der Koffer → den Koffer · ein Brief → einen Brief · die Tasche → die Tasche · das Buch → das Buch
grammar.note_en:
The subject is the person or thing a clause says something about. A direct object is the person or thing directly affected or selected by the verb. In Lina nimmt den Koffer (“Lina takes the suitcase”), Lina is the subject and den Koffer is the direct object. The subject uses the nominative case; this kind of object uses the accusative. Compare Der Koffer ist blau (“The suitcase is blue”), where der Koffer is the subject. German marks that difference in the article even when the noun itself looks unchanged.

For masculine singular nouns, der becomes den and ein becomes einen in the accusative: der Koffer → den Koffer (“the suitcase”), ein Brief → einen Brief (“a letter”). Feminine die/eine and neuter das/ein keep those forms in the accusative: Lina nimmt das Buch (“Lina takes the book”), Emil hat eine Tasche (“Emil has a bag”). Do not turn every der into den: Der Mann hat einen Koffer means “The man has a suitcase”; der Mann is still the subject. Identifying expressions after ist remain nominative: Das ist ein Buch means “That is a book,” not “That takes a book.”

The reading frames hat (“has”), sucht (“looks for”), findet (“finds”), nimmt (“takes”) and sieht (“sees”) take accusative objects in the examples here. Recognise those whole third-person singular forms; this chapter does not ask you to conjugate them or supply them as productive answers. Notice the difference between a search and its outcome: Emil sucht einen Brief (“Emil looks for a letter”), then Mira findet einen Brief (“Mira finds a letter”). The third-person singular forms of nehmen and sehen are nimmt and sieht, not regular-looking forms invented from the infinitive. Full singular conjugation follows in chapter 3.

Kein is the negative counterpart of ein: Emil hat keinen Schlüssel means “Emil has no key / does not have a key.” Use keinen before a masculine accusative noun, keine before a feminine accusative noun, and kein before a neuter accusative noun: kein Buch (“no book”). It is the noun's gender and case that choose the ending. Kein is not a general replacement for nicht: Die Adresse ist nicht richtig (“The address is not correct”) negates the property richtig. The systematic contrast returns later.

Words for properties still stay uninflected after ist: Die Tasche ist leer (“The bag is empty”), Der Name ist richtig (“The name is correct”), Die Adresse ist falsch (“The address is wrong”). At the end the recipient's name matches Lina, while the address points to the empty former shop rather than her occupied home. That distinction drives the new problem; a correct name does not make an address current. The letter and book are separate objects. The small red suitcase remains inside the first house; the blue suitcase and the cloth bag are with Emil. Reference tables collect the article forms shown in these scenes. They are for consultation, not recitation.
